chapters.title: Appendix E: The Self Science Curriculum

assets.topic: Managing Feelings: Monitoring Self-Talk and Finding the Hurt Beneath Anger
assets.visual_frame_description: A leadership training room at a logistics company on a Tuesday evening. Ruth, a 58-year-old executive coach in a cardigan, sits across from Tomas, a 44-year-old warehouse operations manager whose jaw is tight. On the wall screen, Monday's staff-meeting video is frozen at the 04:12 mark, showing Tomas mid-outburst, finger pointed at a young analyst. A notebook on the table is open to a page titled 'Managing Feelings,' with the Self Science skill list handwritten in the margin.
assets.player_mission: As Ruth, coach Tomas through the aftermath of his Monday outburst using the curriculum's managing-feelings tools. Two tasks: get him to catch the self-talk that fueled his explosion, then help him name the feeling underneath the anger and commit to a concrete plan for Thursday's meeting, where the same analyst presents again.
key_concepts: The Self Science curriculum makes self-awareness its first component: students learn to observe themselves, recognize their feelings, and build a vocabulary for those feelings.
Self-awareness includes knowing the relationship between thoughts, feelings, and reactions.
Managing feelings begins with monitoring self-talk to catch negative messages such as internal put-downs.
The curriculum teaches that part of managing a feeling is realizing what lies behind it - for example, the hurt that underlies anger.
Finding ways to handle fears and anxieties, anger, and sadness is an explicit goal of the managing-feelings component.
Handling stress is taught through learning the value of exercise, guided imagery, and relaxation methods.
Insight means identifying patterns in your emotional life and reactions, and recognizing similar patterns in others.
Communications training emphasizes distinguishing between what someone does or says and your own reactions or judgments about it.
Assertiveness means stating your concerns and feelings without anger or passivity.
Personal responsibility includes accepting your feelings and moods and following through on commitments, such as to studying.
The Self Science curriculum derives from Karen F. Stone and Harold Q. Dillehunt's Self Science: The Subject Is Me (Goodyear Publishing, 1978).
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the managing-feelings mechanism of self-talk monitoring: catching internal put-downs and locating the hurt beneath anger lets a person shift from automatic reaction to chosen response. The appendix presents these as teachable skills; Goleman's synthesis claims they generalize to adult settings, a popular-synthesis claim rather than a controlled experiment.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: Tomas, a 44-year-old warehouse operations manager, exploded at 26-year-old analyst Priya in Monday's planning meeting when she questioned his staffing figures, snapping that she did not know what she was talking about and walking out. Priya has told HR she may file a complaint, and Tomas is enrolled in a leadership development series built on the Self Science curriculum. His coach Ruth has one session tonight to convert the incident into a learning moment before Thursday, when Priya presents the revised plan to the same team.
dialogue: RUTH: 'Before we get to what Priya said, let's rewind to the second before you spoke. What was running through your head?'
TOMAS: 'Same as always - She thinks I'm incompetent. Everyone in this room can see it.' It just went off after that.
RUTH: 'That inner voice is your self-talk. The managing-feelings unit says to monitor it for messages that put you down. Now, what feeling is underneath that thought?'
TOMAS: 'Honestly? Humiliation. Like the team thinks I'm a relic who can't do the numbers.'
RUTH: 'Good - you found it. That's the point of the exercise: locating the hurt behind the anger. Now watch the clip from 04:12. What does the recording show?'
TOMAS: 'I'm already gone. Red face, finger pointing. The words take a full two seconds to catch up.'
RUTH: 'Right. The reaction fired before you could edit it. Thursday, Priya presents again. How do you want to enter that room?'
choices: Say nothing more tonight; on Thursday, apologize quickly to Priya so she drops the HR threat with HR, and hope the meeting stays calm.
Coach me on catching the self-talk - I should say the put-down thought out loud, name the feeling under it, then lock in a concrete way to respond at Thursday's meeting.
Tell me to just not feel the anger - suppress it the way I did at my last job.
Arrange for someone else to present the plan Thursday so I don't have to face Priya again.
assets.theoretical_principle: Managing feelings through self-talk monitoring - the Self Science curriculum teaches students to monitor their inner speech to catch negative messages such as internal put-downs, and to uncover what lies behind a feeling, such as the hurt that underlies anger, before choosing how to act.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 2 works because it runs the managing-feelings sequence in order: catch the internal put-down, trace the anger to its underlying feeling (humiliation), and convert insight into a concrete behavioral plan - exactly the thoughts-feelings-reactions link the curriculum is built to strengthen. Choice 1 fails because a fast apology without understanding the trigger leaves the hair-trigger intact: the same self-talk will fire Thursday and the HR pressure guarantees a repeat explosion. Choice 3 fails because suppression is not management; the curriculum's tools are about recognizing and working with a feeling, not denying it, and buried anger leaks out later. Choice 4 fails because it substitutes avoidance for the assertiveness and communication skills the curriculum aims to build.

assets.topic: Conflict Resolution: The Win/Win Model and I-Messages
assets.visual_frame_description: A bright hallway of the Cedar Hills Community Health Center in Portland, minutes before a planning meeting. Alyssa, 37, a program coordinator, holds a clipboard with the health-fair staffing plan; Dev, 39, the outreach lead, stands with arms crossed, slightly hunched. A paper schedule with the training slot taped over reads 'Saturday 10:00' in marker. Behind them the meeting room door is open and chairs are being pulled in.
assets.player_mission: As Alyssa, resolve the scheduling conflict with Dev before the meeting starts. Use the curriculum's tools: state your concern without blame, and negotiate toward a win/win outcome instead of accepting a win-lose one or escalating the fight.
key_concepts: Conflict resolution in the Self Science curriculum teaches how to fight fair with other kids, with parents, and with teachers.
The curriculum's conflict-resolution model is a win/win model for negotiating compromise.
Assertiveness means stating your concerns and feelings without anger or passivity.
Communications training teaches sending I-messages instead of blame.
Communications training distinguishes between what someone does or says and your own reactions or judgments about it.
Group dynamics in the curriculum covers cooperation and knowing when and how to lead, and when to follow.
Self-disclosure teaches valuing openness and building trust in a relationship.
Personal decision-making teaches examining your actions and knowing their consequences.
Managing feelings includes finding ways to handle anger once the feeling underneath it is noticed.
The curriculum's empathy component teaches understanding others' feelings and concerns and taking their perspective.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the assertiveness plus win/win negotiation mechanism: replacing blame language with I-messages and trading concrete concessions converts a zero-sum conflict into a compromise both parties can defend. The appendix frames this as a learned skill of the curriculum, part of Goleman's broader synthesis that such competencies can be systematically trained.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: Alyssa and Dev co-lead the Cedar Hills annual community health fair. Dev moved the volunteer training to Saturday morning without telling Alyssa, a slot that collides with her weekend clinic shift, and has already announced it to twelve volunteers. He declares 'it's done' ten minutes before the joint planning meeting. Alyssa is furious, but the meeting is about to start and her staff-development series based on the Self Science curriculum has drilled the win/win model for negotiating compromise.
dialogue: ALYSSA: 'Dev, the Saturday slot doesn't work for me - I'm on clinic shift that morning.'
DEV: 'I already told the volunteers. Twelve people confirmed. Changing it again makes us look disorganized.'
ALYSSA: 'When you announce a change without checking with me, I feel shut out of decisions I'm supposed to co-lead.'
DEV: 'So what do you want - me to un-announce it? That's a mess either way.'
ALYSSA: 'I want a slot that works for both of us instead of accepting a win-lose outcome.'
DEV: 'Okay. The only other open window is Thursday after work - but attendance is always thin then.'
ALYSSA: 'Then let's offer Thursday evening, plus a short recorded version volunteers can watch at home, so the twelve who confirmed still get the full training.'
choices: Accuse him: 'You always steamroll me, Dev. You never check first.' Then storm into the meeting and let the director settle it.
Give in quietly: 'Fine, it's fine. I'll make it work on Saturday somehow,' while fuming inside and planning to vent to the nurses later.
Blend an I-message with a concrete win/win offer: 'I feel cut out when the time changes without me. Thursday evening plus a recorded training covers the twelve who confirmed - can we run with that?'
Escalate: 'I'm taking this to the director. She can overrule you in front of the whole team.'
assets.theoretical_principle: Assertiveness and the win/win model - the Self Science curriculum teaches stating concerns and feelings without anger or passivity, replacing blame with I-messages, and negotiating compromise through a win/win model of fighting fair.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 3 works because it runs two curriculum components in sequence: the I-message ('I feel cut out when...') separates Dev's action from Alyssa's reaction and judgment, and the Thursday-plus-recorded-training proposal is textbook win/win - Dev keeps his twelve confirmations and Alyssa keeps her clinic shift, so neither side loses face. Choice 1 fails because 'you always' is blame language the curriculum explicitly replaces; it attacks the person rather than the act and predictably hardens Dev's position. Choice 2 fails because passive surrender preserves the win-lose outcome the win/win model exists to avoid, and the suppressed resentment is anger that will resurface in later interactions. Choice 4 fails because pulling rank converts a two-party negotiation into an authority contest: it may win the slot but it destroys the trust that the communications and group-dynamics components treat as the base of cooperation.

assets.topic: Mastering the Front Line: Deploying the Self Science Components
assets.visual_frame_description: A principal's observation walk at Bayview Middle School. A 5th-grade classroom where children sit in a circle around a bridge-building project; Jamal and Rosa face each other, Rosa's hand still mid-air from her protest. The principal, Mr. Okonkwo, stands at the back with an observation clipboard listing the thirteen curriculum components. In stage two, the scene shifts to his office desk, covered with student journal cards and a month-calendar marked with open Friday blocks.
assets.player_mission: As Mr. Okonkwo, first diagnose which Self Science component the classroom moment is demanding in real time, then choose the correct next lesson for the class once the journal evidence reveals the actual deficit. Miss the mechanism and the intervention lands on the wrong skill.
key_concepts: The Self Science curriculum consists of components including self-awareness, personal decision-making, managing feelings, handling stress, empathy, communications, self-disclosure, insight, self-acceptance, personal responsibility, assertiveness, group dynamics, and conflict resolution.
Self-awareness means observing yourself and recognizing your feelings, and knowing the relationship between thoughts, feelings, and reactions.
Communications training teaches distinguishing between what someone does or says and your own reactions or judgments about it.
Communications training teaches sending I-messages instead of blame.
Self-disclosure means valuing openness, building trust in a relationship, and knowing when it is safe to risk talking about your private feelings.
Managing feelings includes monitoring self-talk to catch negative messages such as internal put-downs.
Group dynamics means cooperation and knowing when and how to lead, and when to follow.
Empathy means understanding others' feelings and concerns and taking their perspective, and appreciating differences in how people feel about things.
Handling stress includes learning the value of exercise, guided imagery, and relaxation methods.
Personal decision-making means examining your actions and knowing their consequences, and knowing whether thought or feeling is ruling a decision.
The curriculum is designed to be taught school-style: its source is Karen F. Stone and Harold Q. Dillehunt's Self Science curriculum from 1978.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the curriculum-as-system mechanism: each Self Science component names a distinct teachable deficit, and competent application requires diagnosing which component a live moment demands before intervening. The appendix's evidence is the curriculum's own design, presented by Goleman as a working model of emotional-literacy training.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests mastery of the Self Science curriculum as an integrated system: each of its named components - self-awareness, personal decision-making, managing feelings, handling stress, empathy, communications, self-disclosure, insight, self-acceptance, personal responsibility, assertiveness, group dynamics, and conflict resolution - targets a distinct deficit, and a skilled teacher diagnoses which component a moment demands before intervening.
assets.stage_1_observation: Ms. Herrera's Friday-morning Self Science class has paused bridge-building. Jamal, 11, grabbed the glue gun mid-task from his partner Rosa, who protested, 'You always take over everything!' Jamal rolled his eyes and turned his back. Ms. Herrera froze the class and asked, 'Who can describe what just happened using our skills vocabulary?' A girl raises her hand and says Rosa is judging Jamal's action; a boy adds that Jamal shut the conversation down. Mr. Okonkwo watches from the back of the room with the component list on his clipboard.
assets.stage_1_question: Which Self Science component is the class being guided to practice in this exact moment?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: Communications - the students are being led to separate what Jamal did from Rosa's judgment of it ('you always' is a judgment, not an observation), which is the curriculum's communications skill of distinguishing what someone does from your reactions and judgments, and replacing blame with I-messages.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Two weeks later, Okonkwo reviews journal cards from the same class: six of 27 students wrote that they keep feelings private because kids at school will use them against you, and lunch-period conflicts among those six are climbing. Ms. Herrera asks which lesson to run next Friday: (a) an empathy lesson taking perspectives on a shared story, (b) a group-dynamics exercise on leading versus following, (c) a self-disclosure lesson on building trust and knowing when it is safe to risk talking about private feelings, or (d) a handling-stress unit with guided imagery and relaxation methods.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The self-disclosure lesson - the journal evidence names distrust of openness as the specific deficit, and the curriculum's self-disclosure component teaches valuing openness, building trust in a relationship, and knowing when it is safe to risk talking about private feelings; empathy, group dynamics, and stress methods target different components the evidence does not flag.

chapters.title: Appendix F: Social and Emotional Learning: Results

assets.topic: Weighing the Evidence: Choosing an SEL Program with Comparison Groups
assets.visual_frame_description: Superintendent Maya Chen's office in an Ohio district, evening before the school board vote. Two laptops show vendor decks; a printed stack of evaluation summaries from Goleman's Appendix F sits between her and Derek, the student support director. Derek taps a column labeled 'Evaluation design' while Maya, in glasses, circles notes on a district pilot rubric for three elementary schools.
assets.player_mission: As Superintendent Chen, pressure-test each program's evidence with Derek and choose the pilot program whose evaluation design can survive a school board challenge. The deciding move is sorting programs by who measured the results and against what comparison, not by the size of the claimed gains.
key_concepts: The Child Development Project (Eric Schaps, Oakland) was evaluated in Northern California schools, grades K-6, by independent observers comparing project schools with control schools.
Child Development Project findings included students becoming more responsible, more assertive, more pro-social and helpful, more 'democratic', more harmonious, and better at conflict resolution.
PATHS (Mark Greenberg, Seattle, grades 1-5) was evaluated by teacher ratings comparing matched control students among regular, deaf, and special-education students.
PATHS reported improvements in social cognitive skills, emotion recognition and understanding, self-control, better planning, and more thinking before acting.
Special-needs students in PATHS improved classroom behavior on frustration tolerance, assertive social skills, task orientation, peer skills, sharing, sociability, and self-control.
PATHS participants showed decreases in self-reports of sadness and depression, and decreases in anxiety and withdrawal.
The Seattle Social Development Project (J. David Hawkins) was evaluated by independent testing and objective standards, in comparison to nonprogram schools.

The Seattle Social Development Project found more positive attachment to family and school, less drug-use initiation, less delinquency, and fewer suspensions and expulsions among low-achieving students.
The Resolving Conflict Creatively Program (Linda Lantieri, New York City, grades K-12) was evaluated by teachers' ratings before and after the program, with no comparison group reported.

The Yale-New Haven Social Competence Promotion Program (Roger Weissberg, New Haven grades 5-8) was evaluated by independent observations and student and teacher reports, compared with a control group.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests evaluation-design literacy: the credibility of an SEL claim depends on who measured the outcome and against what comparison, since self-collected pre/post ratings cannot exclude secular improvement. Appendix F compiles programs with designs ranging from independent observers with control schools to teacher-only pre/post ratings, and Goleman's synthesis leans on the stronger designs.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.scenario_setup: Superintendent Maya Chen must recommend one social-emotional learning program to pilot in three elementary schools, and the school board votes in 72 hours. Her past two pilots died when principals could not defend the numbers before the board. Derek has assembled the evaluation summaries compiled in Goleman's Appendix F, and four vendors are in the district office today pushing programs with 'proven results' slides.
dialogue: DEREK: 'Four vendors are here this morning. Three opened with proven-results decks.'
MAYA: 'Show me how they proved it. That is the whole game.'
DEREK: 'The New York conflict-resolution program has glowing teacher ratings - pre-test, post-test, fewer verbal put-downs in class. But there is no comparison group.'
MAYA: 'So we cannot know if the drop was the program or just a good year.'

DEREK: 'Exactly. The Oakland Child Development Project, though, was rated by independent observers against control schools, grades K through 6. The kids came out more pro-social, more assertive, better at conflict resolution.'
MAYA: 'Independent observers with control schools - that design can survive a board challenge. What about PATHS in Seattle?'
DEREK: 'Teacher ratings against matched control students, and it is the one with hard data on special-needs kids - frustration tolerance, task orientation, self-control all improved.'
MAYA: 'Okay. So the strongest evidence is where the measurements were not collected by the people running the classes, and where comparison groups existed.'
choices: Pick the New York program, because its classroom-atmosphere ratings improved and it covers the most grade levels, K-12.
Pick the Oakland Child Development Project, because independent observers rated gains against control schools, giving the board a design argument it can defend.
Pick PATHS, because it improved self-control and emotion recognition, and teachers who know special-needs students best reported the gains.
Kill the pilot and tell the board no program in the appendix is proven well enough to fund.
assets.theoretical_principle: Evidence evaluation under the social-emotional-learning research base: Appendix F compiles programs whose claims rest on different evaluation designs - independent observers with control schools (Child Development Project), teacher ratings with matched controls (PATHS), and objective standards versus nonprogram schools (Seattle) - so the credibility of each claim tracks the strength of its comparison design.
assets.psychological_breakdown: Choice 2 works because it selects the design most robust to challenge: the Child Development Project's gains were rated by independent observers comparing against control schools, which limits the self-report and secular-trend artifacts that plague teacher pre/post ratings - exactly the evidentiary wall the school board will push on. Choice 1 fails because the New York program's results rest on teachers' own pre- and post-ratings with no comparison group, so the board's first question, 'compared to what?', has no answer. Choice 3 fails because although PATHS used matched controls, its outcome measures were teacher ratings - still collected by the people delivering the classrooms - and the district needs an independent check against vendor skepticism. Choice 4 overcorrects: it ignores that several designs in the appendix (independent observers, objective standards, nonprogram comparisons) already meet the district's stated standard; the task is to sort designs, not abandon the field.

assets.topic: The Results Room: Attributing Outcomes to the Right Programs
assets.visual_frame_description: A district evaluation room lined with six monitors, each showing a program summary from Appendix F with its outcome lists displayed as glowing cards. A consultant's desk holds a shuffled deck of result lists; one monitor is flagged with an analyst's incorrect label. In stage two, the scene escalates to an assistant superintendent's desk, where a middle-school transition report is being compared against a card that reads 'followed up into high school.'
assets.player_mission: As the district's evaluation consultant, catch the mislabeled findings in stage one and then, in stage two, attribute the correct longitudinal outcome to its owning program. The battle punishes the classic error of conflating outcome signatures across the six evaluated programs.
key_concepts: PATHS (Mark Greenberg, Fast Track Project, University of Washington) was evaluated in Seattle schools, grades 1-5, by teacher ratings comparing matched control students among regular, deaf, and special-education students.
PATHS special-needs students improved classroom behavior on frustration tolerance, assertive social skills, task orientation, peer skills, sharing, sociability, and self-control.
PATHS participants showed decreases in self-reports of sadness and depression, and decreases in anxiety and withdrawal.

The Improving Social Awareness-Social Problem Solving Project (Maurice Elias, Rutgers) was evaluated in New Jersey schools, grades K-6, by teacher ratings, peer assessments, and school records compared with nonparticipants.
Elias's project found students more sensitive to others' feelings, with a better understanding of the consequences of their behavior.
Elias's project found students better able to size up interpersonal situations and plan appropriate actions, with higher self-esteem and more pro-social behavior.
Students in Elias's project were sought out by peers for help and better handled the transition to middle school.
Elias's project reported less antisocial, self-destructive, and socially disordered behavior even when students were followed up into high school.
The Seattle Social Development Project (J. David Hawkins) was evaluated in Seattle elementary and middle schools by independent testing and objective standards compared to nonprogram schools.

The Seattle Social Development Project found boys less aggressive and girls less self-destructive, fewer suspensions and expulsions among low-achieving students, less drug-use initiation, and less delinquency.

The Yale-New Haven Social Competence Promotion Program (Roger Weissberg, grades 5-8) reported better impulse control, better coping with anxiety, less delinquent behavior, and better conflict-resolution skills.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests accurate attribution of outcome signatures to their source programs: Appendix F assigns each evaluated program its own distinct reported results, and conflation across programs is the central analytical trap. The evidence is a compilation of published evaluations, presented by Goleman with their designs and source citations intact.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.boss_battle_explanation: The battle tests accurate attribution of outcomes to programs: Appendix F is a compilation in which each evaluated program - Child Development Project, PATHS, Seattle Social Development Project, Yale-New Haven Social Competence Promotion, Resolving Conflict Creatively Program, and the Improving Social Awareness-Social Problem Solving Project - has its own outcome signature, and conflating findings across programs is the analytical error the data set punishes.
assets.stage_1_observation: Six monitors in the district evaluation room each show one Appendix F program summary, but an analyst has shuffled the outcome lists. Monitor 3 displays: 'Improved classroom behavior on: frustration tolerance, assertive social skills, task orientation, peer skills, sharing, sociability, self-control,' flagged for special-needs students, plus 'decreases in self-reports of sadness and depression.' The analyst has labeled Monitor 3 'Seattle Social Development Project.' The consultant's notes on the desk list the six true programs and their designs.
assets.stage_1_question: Which program's findings actually produced the special-needs classroom-behavior and emotional-understanding signature shown on Monitor 3?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: PATHS - Appendix F attributes 'improved classroom behavior on frustration tolerance, assertive social skills, task orientation, peer skills, sharing, sociability, self-control' among special-needs students, and decreases in reported sadness and depression with reduced anxiety and withdrawal, to Mark Greenberg's PATHS project in Seattle schools.
assets.stage_2_intervention: The battle escalates: the assistant superintendent, Novak, must recommend a program to a K-6 principal specifically worried about the middle-school transition. Novak reads a claim: students became 'more sensitive to others' feelings,' 'sought out by peers for help,' 'better handled the transition to middle school,' and showed 'less antisocial, self-destructive, and socially disordered behavior, even when followed up into high school.' She asks which program owns this result: PATHS, the Yale-New Haven Social Competence Promotion Program, or the Improving Social Awareness-Social Problem Solving Project run by Maurice Elias at Rutgers.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: The Improving Social Awareness-Social Problem Solving Project - Elias's New Jersey evaluation (grades K-6, teacher ratings, peer assessments, and school records against nonparticipants) is the source of the sensitivity, peer-help-seeking, middle-school transition, and long-term follow-up results in Appendix F; the Yale-New Haven program's signature is impulse control, coping with anxiety, and problem-solving, and PATHS's is emotion recognition and special-needs classroom behavior.

assets.topic: The Vendor's Slide Show: Auditing an Overstated SEL Evaluation
assets.visual_frame_description: A conference room at a district office, a purchasing panel of five across a long table. Roger Ellison, 49, in a fitted blazer, presents from a laptop; behind him a wide screen cycles outcome slides (more empathy, better self-control, fewer put-downs). A panelist's clipboard has a printed copy of the Appendix F evaluation summaries. The room has a wall clock visible over Roger's shoulder.
assets.player_mission: Audit Roger Ellison's claim that his HeartSkills program is independently evaluated. Compare what his behavior and answers reveal against the evaluation designs genuinely documented in Appendix F, then deliver a diagnosis of whether he is overstating his evidence.
key_concepts: The Child Development Project was rated by independent observers who compared project schools with control schools.
The Seattle Social Development Project was evaluated by independent testing and objective standards in comparison to nonprogram schools.
The Yale-New Haven Social Competence Promotion Program was evaluated by independent observations and student and teacher reports compared with a control group.
PATHS compared matched control students using teacher ratings across regular, deaf, and special-education populations.
The Resolving Conflict Creatively Program was evaluated by teachers' ratings, pre- and post-program, with no comparison group reported.
The Improving Social Awareness-Social Problem Solving Project used teacher ratings, peer assessments, and school records compared with nonparticipants.
Elias's project tracked outcomes into high school, reporting less antisocial, self-destructive, and socially disordered behavior in follow-up.
A claim of credibility in Appendix F-style research rests on who measured the outcome and against what comparison group.
Specific, rehearsed figures are what genuine evaluations report; vague, hedged numbers signal unverified claims.
The appendix names its program evaluations with sources and designs, so claims can be checked against a documented evidence base.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the credibility-assessment mechanism of the social-emotional-learning evidence base: claims about program results are only as strong as the measurement design behind them (independent observers, control or matched groups, longitudinal follow-up). The appendix's documented designs supply the yardstick against which the vendor's hedged and self-collected claims are judged.

credibility.basis: Popular synthesis of affective research; EI construct scope debated

assets.question: Is Roger Ellison, founder of HeartSkills Learning, presenting a genuine independent evaluation of his SEL program, or is he claiming results stronger than his evidence supports?
assets.subject_baseline: Roger Ellison, 49, is a seasoned ed-tech sales founder who has pitched districts for twelve years. On his best days he presents relaxed and expansive: leaning back in his chair, hands open, telling warm stories about students, and he is comfortable with hostile finance questions.
observed_nonverbal_log: 0:00-2:00 - Roger opens with a warm story about a fourth grader; steady eye contact, open palms, relaxed posture, a practiced smile.

2:01-4:30 - He names his outcomes (more empathy, better self-control, fewer put-downs in class). When a panelist asks who measured the gains, he glances at his notes for the first time and answers 'teachers in our schools.'

4:31-5:45 - Asked whether there was a control school or a matched comparison, Roger looks down at the table, brings both hands to his collar, and his pace speeds up: 'We, um, gathered pre- and post-data across thirty-one classrooms... a strong body of evidence.'

5:46-8:20 - Asked about independent observers, Roger laughs briefly, shifts in his seat, and answers with a question: 'Wouldn't you trust the teachers who actually know the kids?' He never names an independent evaluator.

8:21-10:00 - Asked whether any finding held into middle school or beyond, Roger squints at the ceiling, says 'somewhere in the teens percent,' then corrects: 'I'd have to get our data team to pull that.' He checks his watch twice.
interrogation_transcript: PANELIST: 'Did an independent observer rate your classrooms, or was that done by your own staff?'
ROGER: 'Our evaluators were extremely thorough - they were in thirty-one classrooms, they know the program inside and out. That's a strength, really.'
PANELIST: 'Was there a comparison group of schools that did not run HeartSkills?'
ROGER: 'We did pre- and post-ratings in every classroom. Any change shows up in that design.'

PANELIST: 'The well-documented programs in the literature - the Child Development Project used independent observers against control schools; Seattle used objective standards against nonprogram schools. Which of those designs applies to your data?'
ROGER: 'Ha - well, those are much bigger projects than ours. Our schools are proud of the numbers they collect.'
PANELIST: 'Do you have any outcome data that survived into high school?'
ROGER: 'We, ah, we've got follow-up numbers... I'd need our data team. Somewhere in the teens, I believe.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: Deception: Roger is materially overstating the evidence. His actual results are self-collected teacher pre/post ratings with no comparison group, while he presents them as credible evaluation outcomes - a gap the genuinely documented programs in Appendix F fill with independent observers, control or matched groups, and longitudinal follow-up.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: The verbal-nonverbal cluster at 4:31-5:45 (dropped gaze, collar touch, accelerated pace, the hedging 'we, um, gathered... a strong body of evidence') marks the comparison-group question as the pressure point, and his answer that 'any change shows up in that design' never actually claims to have had a control school - it sidesteps the absence. The laughter-plus-counter-question at 5:46-8:20 substitutes 'trust the teachers' for independent measurement, exactly the design property that separates his claim from the Child Development Project's independent observers or the Seattle project's objective standards. The watch-checking and 'somewhere in the teens percent' vagueness at 8:21-10:00 reveal the longitudinal claim is neither rehearsed nor real, whereas genuinely reported programs such as Elias's tracked outcomes even into high school. The relaxed baseline at 0:00-2:00 establishes that the tension appears specifically when evaluation design is probed, not from general nervousness.
distractors: He is telling the truth: his program really is independently evaluated, and the panel is being overly cautious.
He is lying about a personal matter - for example, embellishing his own credentials and biography.
He is simply a nervous public speaker whose discomfort at 4:31-5:45 has nothing to do with the substance of his evidence.
